name: Skype Design System
summary: Production-ready SwiftUI design system prompt for a call-first messenger built around Skype Blue, inline call cards, and a video grid.
description: Generates a full design-token set and component library modeled on Skype's call-first identity — cloud-blue brand color, presence dots, inline call-history cards, and a gradient video grid.

whatYouGet: A complete Swift color and type token library matching a call-first cloud-blue identity
Ready-to-paste SwiftUI views for the message bubble, inline call card, video grid, and presence dot
Motion, haptic, and Do/Don't guardrails so an agent can't drift off-brand mid-build
content.promptText:
<role>
You are a senior iOS design-systems engineer who specializes in translating a messaging brand's visual identity into a production SwiftUI token library and component set. You think in exact hex values, point-based spacing scales, and SF Symbols, and you never invent a value you weren't given.
</role>

<reference_data>
Brand anchor: a bright cloud-cyan "call-first" blue at #00AFF0, with a deeper text-safe variant #0078D4 used anywhere white text sits on top (outgoing bubble, filled surfaces needing AA contrast). Pressed state #0091CC; a lighter accent #34C3FF serves gradients and dark-mode links.
Canvas: pure white #FFFFFF in light mode; a neutral near-black #16161A in dark mode — deliberately not color-tinted, so the brand blue stays vivid against it. Surface tiers #F4F4F6 (light) / #1F1F24 and #2A2A30 (dark, two elevation steps). Dividers #E2E2E6 light / #34343C dark.
Text: primary #1B1B1F light / #F2F2F4 dark, secondary #6E6E78 / #A4A4AE, tertiary #9A9AA4 / #6F6F79. Text on the bright accent button must use a deep-cyan ink #00343F, not white, to pass WCAG AA — white is reserved for text on the deep #0078D4 surface.
Semantic: accept-call/online green #2DC26B, end-call/destructive/unread-badge red #E8364F, away-presence yellow #FFC400.
Type ladder: a rounded, confidently heavy humanist sans (the brand face is proprietary; Inter or Open Sans are the free substitutes), weights concentrated at 400 body / 600-700 emphasis / 700-800 titles. Large title 32/800, headline 17/700, body 15/400, caption 11/600, button 16/700.
Corner radii: 4pt tail-pinch on a bubble corner, 8pt subtle, 14pt standard (bubbles, call cards, video tiles), 18pt input fields and sheets, 22pt (or full pill) for primary CTAs, 50% for avatars and call-control circles.
Distinctive named patterns: (1) presence dots on every avatar — filled green/yellow/red, or a hollow gray ring for offline; (2) inline call cards interleaved directly in the message thread, showing a phone glyph, duration, and participant count; (3) an adaptive video-call grid with gradient-fallback tiles, a small pinned self-view, and per-tile mute indicators; (4) a heart-led emoji reaction strip that docks as a small chip on a bubble after a long-press; (5) a bottom control bar of large 52-56pt circular buttons for mute/video/share/end-call.
</reference_data>

<house_rules>
1. The accent blue has two distinct faces, never one: bright #00AFF0 is for interactive chrome (buttons, tabs, FABs); deep #0078D4 is reserved for the outgoing bubble and any surface that needs white text on top. Never swap them.
2. Never place white text directly on the bright #00AFF0 button — it fails contrast. Use the deep-cyan ink token there instead.
3. Dark mode stays neutral, never brand-tinted — resist casting the dark canvas toward blue; that neutrality is what keeps the accent legible against it.
4. Every avatar carries a presence indicator by default unless the context has no concept of "online" at all — visible people-status is the whole identity of this app.
5. Calling affordances are never optional or buried in a menu — a phone glyph and a video glyph belong in every one-to-one chat header, full stop.
6. Completed calls are never a separate log the user has to dig for — every call becomes an inline card living in the same scrollback as messages.
7. Reactions dock as a small chip overlapping a bubble's corner; they never create a second full-width row beneath the message.
8. Reserve shadows for genuinely floating surfaces (menus, sheets, the reaction strip); bubbles, list rows, and call cards stay flat with zero elevation.
9. Motion stays soft and quick — 150-320ms springs — nothing overshoots aggressively or lingers past half a second.
</house_rules>

<the_project>
App name: [your app name]
Primary platform target: [iOS / iOS+iPadOS / cross-platform via SwiftUI]
Brand accent hex (if different from the reference): [hex or "use reference as-is"]
Minimum iOS version: [e.g. iOS 17]
Which screens do you need first: [chat thread / video call / contacts / all]
Existing design tokens to reconcile against (paste any current Color/Font extensions): [paste or "none, starting fresh"]
Any brand constraints that override the reference (e.g. no gradients allowed, different corner-radius scale): [describe or "none"]
</the_project>

<what_to_give_me>
1. A complete `Color` extension (light + dark adaptive variants) covering every token in the reference data, named clearly by role, not by hex.
2. A `Font` extension implementing the full type ladder with the specified weights and sizes, using the named substitute typeface.
3. SwiftUI views for the message bubble (incoming + outgoing, with the tail-pinch corner and grouping/gap rules), the inline call card, and the presence dot component.
4. A SwiftUI view for the adaptive video-call grid plus the bottom circular control bar, including the self-view tile and per-tile mute indicator.
5. A short motion/haptics reference (spring parameters, durations, haptic triggers) matching the reference data's timing.
6. A one-page Do/Don't checklist an engineer can paste at the top of a PR description to self-review before merging.
7. Flag anywhere you had to guess a value not covered by the reference data, rather than silently inventing one.
</what_to_give_me>

Run it in Claude or your AI assistant of choice
Paste the generated SwiftUI tokens/components into your project and adjust to your actual brand constraints

SwiftUI components for the message row, reaction chip, thread indicator, and Huddles banner
A workspace-theming pattern so the sidebar accent is a single swappable variable, not a hardcode
content.promptText:
<role>
You are a senior iOS design-systems engineer specializing in workspace/collaboration apps where a customer-facing brand color must coexist with per-tenant customization. You produce exact Swift tokens and componentized SwiftUI views, never vague guidance.
</role>

<reference_data>
Brand anchor: a deep wine-purple "aubergine" #4A154B as the default sidebar background (pressed state #3F0E40), but this sidebar color is workspace-customizable — treat it as a variable, with alternate presets such as a dark-gray "Monument" #2C2D30, an orange "Tangerine" #CA4400, and a mustard "Ochre" #8B6A05, each with their own active-row accent.
A four-color logo pinwheel exists (#ECB22E yellow, #E01E5A pink, #2EB67D green, #36C5F0 blue) used in the logo and huddle iconography, but rarely elsewhere in chrome.
Content canvas: clean white #FFFFFF light / charcoal #1A1D21 dark (a near-black with warmth, not pure black). Surface tiers #F8F8F8 / #222529, #2C2D30 for sheets/thread-pane on dark. Dividers #DDDDDD / #35373B.
Text: primary #1D1C1D / #D1D2D3, secondary #616061 / #ABABAD. On the sidebar itself: inactive channel names are a muted lavender-white #CFC3CF, active/unread channel names go full white #FFFFFF.
Semantic: online-presence green #007A5A (a darker, more saturated green than the pinwheel green, chosen for dot legibility), mention/urgent pink-red #E01E5A, huddle/typing/link blue #1264A3.
Inline mention pills carry role-specific tinted backgrounds: a green-tinted pill for @channel, a yellow-tinted pill for @here, a red-tinted pill for a specific @user.
Type ladder: a rounded geometric sans (brand face is proprietary; a clean grotesque like Inter or a similar humanist sans substitutes) restricted to two weights, 400 and 700 (with 600 for reaction counts/thread links) — no light or black weights anywhere. Username 15/700, body 15/400 at 1.5 line-height, timestamp 12/400, tab label 11/600.
Corner radii: 4pt (the signature — buttons and, notably, avatars, which are rounded squares, not circles), 8pt (search field, settings rows), 12pt (sheets/modals), 500pt/pill (reaction chips, mention pills).
Distinctive named patterns: (1) rounded-square avatars, never circular — the single biggest visual tell versus other messengers; (2) inline emoji reaction chips below every message, with an outlined "you reacted" state; (3) a thread indicator link ("N replies, last reply Xh ago") that opens a slide-in pane — full-screen on phone, a side pane on tablet; (4) a colored Huddles banner across the top of an active audio-huddle channel; (5) a user status row combining a custom emoji with up to 30 characters of free text next to the person's name everywhere they appear.
</reference_data>

<house_rules>
1. The sidebar accent is a variable, never a hardcoded literal — architect theming so swapping the whole sidebar palette (background, active-row tint, pressed state) is a single config change.
2. The saturated sidebar color never leaks onto the content canvas — the canvas and thread pane stay neutral white/charcoal regardless of which sidebar theme is active.
3. Avatars are always rounded squares, never circles — this is non-negotiable and the single most identity-defining shape decision in the system.
4. Every reaction renders as an inline pill chip (emoji + count) directly under the message body, never as a separate panel or a modal-only affordance.
5. Threads are first-class, not an afterthought: any message with replies shows the thread-link affordance, and opening it is a sliding pane, never a full replace-the-view navigation.
6. Each of the three mention-pill colors is semantically fixed — never let @channel, @here, and a specific @user share a color, and never introduce a fourth mention color.
7. Keep shadows nearly absent — this system is flat by default; elevation exists only for genuinely ephemeral floating UI like an emoji picker or a bottom sheet.
8. Typography never exceeds two working weights (400/700, with 600 as a narrow exception for reactions/thread text) — resist the temptation to add a light or heavy weight for "emphasis."
9. A live audio huddle gets a persistent colored banner at the top of the channel — never bury an active call state inside a menu.
</house_rules>

<the_project>
App name: [your app name]
Primary platform target: [iOS / iOS+iPadOS / cross-platform via SwiftUI]
Default sidebar/brand accent hex (if different from the reference default): [hex or "use aubergine as default"]
Should the sidebar color be end-user customizable: [yes / no]
Minimum iOS version: [e.g. iOS 17]
Which screens do you need first: [sidebar/workspace switcher / channel thread / thread pane / all]
Existing design tokens to reconcile against (paste any current Color/Font extensions): [paste or "none, starting fresh"]
</the_project>

<what_to_give_me>
1. A `Color` extension implementing the sidebar palette as a themeable struct (not hardcoded literals) plus the fixed canvas/text/semantic tokens.
2. A `Font` extension implementing the two-weight type ladder at the specified sizes.
3. SwiftUI views for the message row (rounded-square avatar, username, timestamp, body, reaction-chip row) and the reaction chip itself with its "you reacted" outlined state.
4. A SwiftUI view for the thread indicator link and the sliding thread pane (full-screen phone / side-pane tablet variants).
5. A SwiftUI view for the mention pill (three semantic variants) and the Huddles banner.
6. A short Do/Don't checklist an engineer can use to self-review a PR against this system before merging.
7. Flag anywhere you had to guess a value not covered by the reference data, rather than silently inventing one.
</what_to_give_me>

whatYouGet: A Swift token library architected so accent color is one swappable variable across every surface

content.promptText:
<role>
You are a senior iOS design-systems engineer who specializes in building messengers where the entire color system is end-user themeable, not just the outgoing bubble. You produce exact Swift tokens and componentized SwiftUI views, and you architect for swap-ability from the start.
</role>

<reference_data>
Default accent: a confident sky blue #0088CC (lighter variant #40A7E3 for selection/toggle-on states), but the entire UI is built as a themeable surface — the accent is one variable a user can repoint to any hex, with a preset palette that includes a mint green #3FC1B0, a rose #FF5C77, an orange #FB8C4A, a purple #6F7BF7, and others. Outgoing bubble default #2B86FD (some gradient themes run #2B86FD to #61B3FF).
Canvas: true white #FFFFFF light / a crushed near-black #212121 standard dark, with an optional pure #000000 OLED mode as a separate toggle from standard dark. Surface tiers #F7F7F7 / #1C1C1C, #2C2C2E for sheets on dark.
Bubbles: outgoing default #2B86FD with white text; incoming #FFFFFF light (with a 1pt #E5E5E5 border, visible against a plain wallpaper) / #2A2A2A dark, with primary text color.
Text: primary #000000 light / #FFFFFF dark, secondary #707579 / #8D8E93.
Semantic: read-receipt tick color matches the accent (not a separate hue), sent-tick gray #B1B1B1, error red #E53935, online-presence green #4DD364, a premium purple gradient #AE6FFD to #CE6BFF for premium badges/reactions.
Sender-name colors in group chats rotate through a fixed seven-color palette for scannability (e.g. #FC5C51, #FA790F, #895DD5, #0FB297).
Type ladder: pure SF Pro at strict iOS HIG sizes — no proprietary typeface at all. Bubble body 17/400, contact name 17/600, timestamp-in-bubble 11/400, tab label 10/500. A monospace face renders code blocks.
Corner radii: bubbles use 17pt on every corner EXCEPT the tail corner, which drops to a 6pt soft notch — never a fully pointed tail. Primary sheet CTAs sit at 10pt, the floating voice-player and reaction palette at 20-28pt/pill.
Distinctive named patterns: (1) fully themeable chat backgrounds per-conversation (solid, gradient, pattern tile, or photo); (2) a swipe-from-edge (not swipe-on-row) gesture that pans the whole bubble sideways to trigger a reply, with a ~60pt drag threshold; (3) a persistent floating pill mini-player for voice messages/music that survives across chat switches; (4) large Lottie-style animated-emoji/sticker playback when a message is a single emoji or a sticker; (5) a long-press-the-send-button popover offering silent send, scheduled send, and send-when-online; (6) secret chats with a self-destruct timer and a screenshot notification to the sender.
</reference_data>

<house_rules>
1. Architect the accent color as a single source-of-truth variable from day one — every blue-tinted surface (links, active tab, outgoing bubble default, buttons) must re-derive from it, because the whole product depends on users re-theming it.
2. Bubbles are flat with zero shadow — reserve elevation exclusively for detached floating elements: the voice mini-player and the long-press context-menu popover.
3. The bubble's tail corner is a soft 6pt notch, never a fully pointed triangle — this is a deliberate, recognizable departure from a sharper competitor's tail shape.
4. Reply is triggered by panning the entire bubble from a screen edge, not by swiping the row — don't conflate the two gesture models.
5. The send button's long-press must surface silent-send and scheduled-send options — this is a core differentiator and should never be cut for scope reasons.
6. Read-receipt ticks recolor to the theme's accent when read, never to a fixed green — that hue is reserved for a different competitor's identity.
7. OLED pure-black is a distinct opt-in mode from standard dark mode, not the default dark theme — keep the two as separate settings.
8. Respect per-chat custom backgrounds as first-class: a solid color, gradient, tiled pattern, or photo, configurable independently of the global theme.
9. Single-emoji or sticker messages render large and animated (not inside a bubble chrome) — typography is allowed to escape its normal frame for this one case.
</house_rules>

<the_project>
App name: [your app name]
Primary platform target: [iOS / iOS+iPadOS / cross-platform via SwiftUI]
Default accent hex (if different from the reference default): [hex or "use sky blue as default"]
Should end users be able to re-theme the accent and chat backgrounds: [yes / no]
Minimum iOS version: [e.g. iOS 17]
Which screens do you need first: [chat thread / compose bar / voice player / secret chat / all]
Existing design tokens to reconcile against (paste any current Color/Font extensions): [paste or "none, starting fresh"]
</the_project>

<what_to_give_me>
1. A `Color` extension architected around a single swappable `accent` variable, plus the fixed canvas/text/semantic tokens and the OLED-mode variant.
2. A `Font` extension implementing the pure SF Pro type ladder at HIG sizes.
3. SwiftUI views for the outgoing/incoming bubble (17pt corners, 6pt tail-notch) and the swipe-from-edge-to-reply gesture handler.
4. A SwiftUI view for the floating voice/music mini-player pill and the animated single-emoji/sticker playback treatment.
5. A SwiftUI implementation of the long-press-send popover (silent send / scheduled send / send-when-online).
6. A short Do/Don't checklist an engineer can use to self-review a PR against this system before merging.
7. Flag anywhere you had to guess a value not covered by the reference data, rather than silently inventing one.
</what_to_give_me>

name: Threema Design System
summary: SwiftUI design system prompt for a privacy-first messenger anchored on a single green and a three-dot trust-level indicator.
description: Generates a Swift token library and component set modeled on Threema's calm, Swiss-engineered identity — one brand green, a monospaced anonymous ID, and the signature red/orange/green trust-dot verification ritual.

whatYouGet: A Swift token library built around exactly one brand accent plus a dedicated three-level trust palette
SwiftUI components for the trust-level dot indicator, the QR verify card, and the monospaced-ID chip
Accessibility-first patterns ensuring trust state is never conveyed by color alone
content.promptText:
<role>
You are a senior iOS design-systems engineer who specializes in privacy- and security-focused products where restraint and legibility of trust state matter more than visual flourish. You produce exact Swift tokens and componentized SwiftUI views, and you treat accessibility labeling as a first-class deliverable, not an afterthought.
</role>

<reference_data>
Brand anchor: a single confident green #088A29 (brightened to #1FA53C for legibility on the dark canvas) — there is no second brand accent anywhere in the system. Pressed state #066B20.
Canvas: pure white #FFFFFF light / dark charcoal #121212 dark — calm and utilitarian, never off-white or warm-tinted. Surface tiers #F4F4F6 / #1C1C1E, #262628 (dark, second elevation). Dividers #E2E2E5 / #2C2C2E.
Text: primary (near-black, not pure black) #111113 / #ECECEC, secondary #6B6B70 / #9A9A9F.
Bubbles: incoming neutral gray #EBEBED / #262628; outgoing a soft green tint of the brand #D6F0DC light / a deep green #0C5E22 dark — never the same hue as incoming.
The signature trust-level palette (three fixed roles, never reused elsewhere except for consistent semantic reuse): Level 1 unverified red #E5453A, Level 2 address-book-matched orange #EF8B2C, Level 3 in-person-QR-verified green #15A33A. An empty/inactive dot slot uses #D2D2D7 light / #3A3A3E dark. Destructive actions share the same red as Level 1 (#E5453A) — deliberately, so "untrusted" and "destructive" read as one consistent hue.
Type ladder: pure SF Pro (no custom typeface at all — the system font is a deliberate choice signaling "we don't distract from the content"), plus SF Mono reserved exclusively for the anonymous ID string and key fingerprint so ambiguous characters (0/O, 1/l) are never confused when read aloud. Large title 32/800, message body 16/400, the monospaced ID field 14/600 with 1pt letter-spacing.
Corner radii: 4pt (tail-pinch, small chips), 8pt (ID chip, search field), 10pt (buttons, grouped table cells, the QR card), 16pt (message bubbles, sheets), full pill (pill buttons, the composer field, unread badge).
Distinctive named patterns: (1) a horizontal row of three same-colored dots next to every contact and conversation, encoding trust level, always paired with a text label so it is never color-only; (2) an anonymous 8-character alphanumeric identity string shown in monospace everywhere, with no phone number or email as an alternative; (3) a QR-code verify flow — scan a contact's code in person to upgrade them to three green dots, with a success animation and haptic; (4) an unverified-contact warning banner (orange left-rule) sitting above the composer until the user verifies; (5) an encrypted-call screen showing a lock glyph plus a short spoken verification phrase both parties can read aloud.
</reference_data>

<house_rules>
1. There is exactly one brand accent — never introduce a second saturated color for anything that isn't the trust palette or a standard system-red destructive action.
2. The three trust-dot colors are fixed roles (red = unverified, orange = address-book-matched, green = in-person-verified) and must never be reassigned to mean anything else in the product.
3. Trust state is never color-only — every trust-dot row ships with an adjacent text label and a combined VoiceOver string; treat this as a hard accessibility requirement, not a nice-to-have.
4. The anonymous ID and any cryptographic fingerprint render exclusively in the monospaced token — never in the proportional body font — so characters read unambiguously aloud.
5. Level 3 (fully verified, green) can only be reached through the explicit in-person QR-scan flow — never auto-upgrade a contact based on any other signal.
6. Keep the whole system nearly flat — shadows exist only to signal "this floats, tap outside to dismiss" (context menus, sheets), never as decoration on bubbles or list rows.
7. Motion stays quiet and short — 120-300ms ease-out transitions; nothing bounces or lingers to draw attention away from content.
8. Never request a phone number or email as an identity primitive in any generated flow — the anonymous ID is the whole identity model.
9. Destructive red and Level-1 (untrusted) red intentionally share the same hex — preserve that overlap rather than giving destructive actions their own separate red.
</house_rules>

<the_project>
App name: [your app name]
Primary platform target: [iOS / iOS+iPadOS / cross-platform via SwiftUI]
Brand accent hex (if different from the reference): [hex or "use reference green as-is"]
Minimum iOS version: [e.g. iOS 17]
Which screens do you need first: [chat thread / verify-contact QR flow / my-ID card / all]
Existing design tokens to reconcile against (paste any current Color/Font extensions): [paste or "none, starting fresh"]
Any accessibility requirements beyond WCAG AA (e.g. specific VoiceOver phrasing already in use): [describe or "none, follow the reference"]
</the_project>

<what_to_give_me>
1. A `Color` extension covering the single brand accent, canvas/text tokens, and the three-role trust palette with its inactive-slot variant.
2. A `Font` extension implementing the SF Pro type ladder plus the SF Mono identity/fingerprint style.
3. A SwiftUI trust-level-dot component (three colored circles + label + combined VoiceOver string) and the monospaced ID chip.
4. A SwiftUI QR-verify card and scanner view, including the reticle animation and the crossfade-to-green success state.
5. SwiftUI views for the incoming/outgoing message bubble and the unverified-contact warning banner.
6. A short Do/Don't checklist an engineer can use to self-review a PR against this system before merging, with special attention to the accessibility rule.
7. Flag anywhere you had to guess a value not covered by the reference data, rather than silently inventing one.
</what_to_give_me>

name: Viber Design System
summary: SwiftUI design system prompt for a call-first purple messenger with a three-state check receipt and a borderless sticker economy.
description: Generates a Swift token library and component set modeled on Viber's purple identity — an aubergine-tinted dark mode, the gray-to-violet three-state read receipt, and full-storefront sticker rendering.

whatYouGet: A Swift token library covering the single purple brand accent, its purple-tinted (not neutral) dark mode, and the receipt-state palette
SwiftUI components for the three-state check receipt, the free-call gradient banner, and borderless in-thread stickers
A sticker-market storefront layout spec and call-first chat-header pattern
content.promptText:
<role>
You are a senior iOS design-systems engineer who specializes in call-first messaging apps where a single saturated brand color must dominate every CTA while a large media economy (stickers) renders cleanly beside it. You produce exact Swift tokens and componentized SwiftUI views.
</role>

<reference_data>
Brand anchor: a single purple #7360F2 used as the entire brand — outgoing bubble, every CTA, tab selection, and the call screen. Deeper variant #665CAC for the wordmark/gradients, pressed state #5B4ACC, a lighter violet #8F7DF7 used specifically for the "seen" receipt state and dark-mode links. A deep-violet #59267C is reserved as the bottom stop of the free-call banner's gradient.
Canvas: white #FFFFFF light / an aubergine-TINTED near-black #121118 dark — deliberately not neutral gray, so the purple cast carries into dark mode. Surface tiers #F4F3F8 / #1C1A24, #26232F (dark, second elevation). Dividers #E4E2EC / #322F3C.
Text: primary #1A1825 / #F3F1F8, secondary #7D7A8C / #9D98AC, tertiary #A8A5B5 / #6C6779 (also used for the single-check "sent" glyph).
Bubbles: outgoing solid purple #7360F2 with white text always; incoming a light lavender-gray #EDEBF5 / #26232F dark.
The signature three-state check receipt: sending shows a clock glyph; sent shows one gray check (#A8A5B5/#6C6779); delivered shows two gray checks (#7D7A8C/#9D98AC); seen recolors both checks to violet #8F7DF7 — this violet recolor is the product's most recognized affordance. Failed send shows a red #F0506E exclamation.
Semantic: online/accept green #46C26A, decline/destructive/unread-badge red #F0506E.
Type ladder: a friendly, heavy-leaning rounded humanist sans (brand face proprietary; Manrope or Nunito Sans substitute), weights concentrated at 400 body / 600-700 emphasis / 700-800 titles.
Corner radii: 5pt tail-pinch, 10pt subtle (search/thumbnails), 14pt standard (banner, cards, reply-quote), 16pt bubble body, 20pt comfortable (sticker cards, sheets), 24pt/pill for CTAs, 50% circle for avatars/send button/call controls.
Distinctive named patterns: (1) the three-state check receipt with its gray-to-violet "seen" recolor; (2) a purple-to-deep-violet gradient "Free Viber Call" banner sitting above the composer, nudging toward free voice/video calling; (3) a full sticker-market storefront reachable from the composer's emoji glyph, with stickers rendering in-thread as large borderless artwork (no bubble chrome at all); (4) call-first chrome — phone and video icons in every chat header plus a dedicated Calls tab; (5) a reactions strip led by a thumbs-up emoji, appearing on long-press.
</reference_data>

<house_rules>
1. Purple #7360F2 is the entire brand — never introduce a second saturated accent; green and red exist only as semantic (online/destructive) signals, never as decoration.
2. Dark mode carries a deliberate aubergine/purple tint in its near-black canvas — do not flatten it to a neutral gray, that tint is intentional brand-carrying.
3. The "seen" receipt state must recolor to violet #8F7DF7, never stay gray — that recolor is the single most recognizable Viber affordance and must not be skipped or simplified to a generic double-check.
4. Stickers render borderless at roughly 96pt, with zero bubble background — never wrap a sticker or animated GIF in the standard message-bubble chrome.
5. The purple-to-deep-violet gradient is reserved strictly for the call screen and the free-call banner — never apply it as a general-purpose decorative background elsewhere.
6. Calling stays one tap away at all times — phone and video icons belong in every chat header, plus a dedicated Calls tab in the primary navigation.
7. Outgoing-bubble text is always white on the solid purple fill — never substitute a dark ink for contrast reasons; adjust the purple's lightness instead if contrast is a concern.

content.promptText:
<role>
You are a senior iOS design-systems engineer who specializes in super-app architectures where a single messaging shell must host many unrelated feature surfaces without visual fatigue. You produce exact Swift tokens and componentized SwiftUI views, and you default to restraint over decoration.
</role>

<reference_data>
Brand anchor: a single green #07C160 (pressed #06A050) used with extreme discipline — send-ready actions, primary buttons, the active tab, toggles, and "pay" affordances only. It is explicitly NOT the outgoing-bubble color.
Canvas: a light-gray chat backdrop #EDEDED, with white #FFFFFF cards, rows, and incoming bubbles sitting on top of it. Surface #F7F7F7 for search/secondary fills. Divider #D9D9D9. A limited dark variant exists: dark canvas #1A1A1A, dark backdrop #111111, dark incoming bubble #2C2C2C, dark outgoing bubble a muted #3EB575.
Text: primary near-black #181818, secondary #888888, tertiary #B2B2B2 — deliberately rationed; almost nothing else in the UI carries color except icon chips, the red dot, and links.
Bubbles: incoming solid white #FFFFFF; outgoing a PALE, slightly acidic chat-green #95EC69 — this is explicitly a different, lighter hue from the brand green, never the brand green itself. Both bubble text colors stay near-black #181818, never white-on-green.
Semantic: a universal red-dot/badge #FA5151 used for unread counts, attention states, and the red-packet card; link-blue #576B95 for inline links and social-post author names.
Per-feature icon accents exist ONLY inside the grouped hub's icon chips (never in general chrome): a blue, a light blue, an orange, a green, an indigo, and a red, each assigned to one specific hub feature.
Type ladder: PingFang SC (Apple's CJK system face) with a Noto Sans Latin fallback, restricted to exactly two weights — 400 regular and 600 semibold — and a single DOMINANT body size of 17pt shared across contact names, list-row titles, and message bodies, for a deliberately calm, uniform scan rhythm.
Corner radii: a notably SQUARER silhouette than most Western messengers — 4pt for a compact send button, 6pt as the dominant standard (bubbles, primary/outline buttons, search field, composer), 8pt for rounded-square avatars and icon chips, 50% reserved only for a small "open" seal coin and a few status dots. Large pill radii are deliberately avoided almost everywhere.
Distinctive named patterns: (1) a grouped list of feature rows (a super-app "hub") gathering unrelated modules — each row a 56pt white surface with a colored square icon chip, a title, and a trailing chevron, clustered by gray gutters; (2) rounded-square avatars (~8pt radius) everywhere, never circles; (3) a red envelope-shaped monetary gift card with a centered gold "open" seal that animates when tapped; (4) a universal small red-dot badge as the single loudest attention primitive on tabs, rows, and avatars; (5) centered time-separator chips between message runs instead of a per-bubble timestamp.
</reference_data>

<house_rules>
1. The brand green is rationed to "go" actions only — send, pay, primary CTA, active tab, toggles — and must never be used for the outgoing message bubble.
2. The outgoing bubble is a distinct pale chat-green, never the brand green and never a bold saturated fill — both bubble text colors stay near-black, not white.
3. Avatars are rounded squares (~8pt radius) everywhere in the system, never circles — this is a constant, non-negotiable brand tell across every surface.
4. Bubbles stay tight and squarer (6pt radius) with a small triangular tail, deliberately less rounded than a typical Western messenger's bubble.
5. Timestamps are never attached to individual bubbles — use a centered time-separator chip between time-grouped runs instead.
6. Hold to exactly two type weights (400/600) and one dominant 17pt body size across names, list rows, and message text — resist adding a third size or weight for "hierarchy"; hierarchy here comes from weight and position, not scale.
7. A per-feature icon color is contained strictly to the hub's grouped-list icon chips — it must never leak into tab bars, headers, or general chrome.
8. The red-dot badge is the loudest element in the whole system on purpose — it should visually outrank any other emphasis technique when something needs attention.
9. Motion is nearly absent by design — a quick fade on send, an instant tab switch, no elaborate transitions — except the one deliberate flourish: the red-packet's opening animation.
</house_rules>

content.promptText:
<role>
You are a senior iOS design-systems engineer who specializes in making a messenger feel indistinguishable from a native iOS system app — deferring to Apple HIG type scales, SF Symbols, and native gesture conventions wherever the brand doesn't demand otherwise. You produce exact Swift tokens and componentized SwiftUI views.
</role>

<reference_data>
Brand system has two stops: a verb-color green #25D366 (pressed #1EBE5D) reserved for send/record/answer/positive actions, and a legacy brand teal #075E54 (mid-teal #128C7E, dark teal #054D44) seen on QR/brand chrome and older screens.
The single most load-bearing color in the whole system is the outgoing-bubble mint-leaf tint #D9FDD3 light / a deep teal-green #005C4B dark — recognizable even as an isolated pixel. Incoming bubble #FFFFFF light / a muted blue-gray #1F2C34 dark.
Canvas is distinct from chat wallpaper: app canvas #FFFFFF light / a blue-black #111B21 dark (never true black — that would wash out the mint bubble); the chat wallpaper itself is a separate cream doodle pattern #ECE5DD light / a deep blue-black #0B141A dark, customizable per chat.
Text: primary #111B21 / #E9EDEF, secondary #667781 / #8696A0.
Read-receipt system: single gray tick #8696A0 = sent, double gray = delivered, double BLUE tick #53BDEB = read — this blue is the single most semantically loaded, non-repurposable color in the app.
Semantic: error/decline red #F15C6D, status-ring green #25D366 for unread Status updates (gray #8696A0 once viewed).
Type ladder: pure SF Pro Text/Display, zero proprietary typeface, weights limited to 400/500/600/700 (no 300, no 800) — large title 34/700, contact name 17/600, bubble body 17/400, timestamp 11-12/400 fixed regardless of Dynamic Type.
Corner radii: bubbles round to 12pt on every corner EXCEPT the corner nearest the sender, which drops to 0pt for a hard asymmetric tail nub — a very different silhouette from a fully-rounded or notched-tail competitor. Compose field 20-24pt pill, search/settings rows 10pt, avatars/send button/status ring full circle.
Distinctive named patterns: (1) the asymmetric-tail bubble (rounded everywhere but one hard corner); (2) a voice-message bubble rendered as a horizontal amplitude waveform with a play/pause circle, where played bars recolor green left-to-right in sync with playback; (3) a green ring around an avatar that segments into arcs for multiple unread Status updates; (4) a persistent end-to-end-encryption lock banner as the very first message in every new chat; (5) a circular send button that morphs between a microphone glyph (empty field) and a paper-plane glyph (text present), with a decibel-responsive expanding ring during a hold-to-record.
</reference_data>

<house_rules>
1. Default to native iOS conventions everywhere the brand doesn't explicitly override them — Dynamic Type, SF Symbols, native swipe-actions, `.regularMaterial` blur on bars — this app succeeds by feeling like part of the OS, not a custom skin on top of it.
2. The mint-leaf outgoing-bubble color is untouchable — never substitute a different green, and never let the bubble surface use the brand teal instead.
3. Chat wallpaper and app canvas are two separate token families — never conflate the cream/dark wallpaper behind the thread with the plain white/blue-black canvas used on list and settings screens.
4. The bubble tail is asymmetric — round every corner except a single 0pt corner nearest the sender; never apply a uniform radius or a soft notch to all four corners.
5. The blue double-check read-receipt color is fixed and never repurposed for anything else in the system, including links, buttons, or badges.
6. Green is structural, not decorative — it only ever means send, answer-call, record, unread-status-ring, or a read-adjacent success signal; never use it as plain accent text or a background fill elsewhere.
7. Dark mode's canvas is a blue-black, never a true black — pure black would flatten the mint-leaf bubble's contrast and read as visually broken.
8. The end-to-end-encryption banner is mandatory as the first message in a brand-new conversation — never skip or relocate it.
9. Keep the whole system nearly shadow-free — a 1-2pt whisper of shadow under a bubble at most; real elevation is reserved for the reaction palette and bottom sheets only.
</house_rules>

content.promptText:
<role>
You are a senior iOS design-systems engineer who specializes in super-app messengers serving a specific-language user base, where typography must correctly render stacked diacritics and a single header color must persist as a constant frame across many unrelated modules. You produce exact Swift tokens and componentized SwiftUI views.
</role>

<reference_data>
Brand anchor: a single blue #0068FF (pressed #0052CC, deep #0047B3) applied with total consistency as the solid background of every screen's top header bar, the primary CTA, the active tab, and the send button — there is no second brand color anywhere in chrome.
Canvas: white #FFFFFF content surface, with the chat thread specifically sitting on a calm blue-grey backdrop #E8ECF1 (distinct from the plain white canvas used elsewhere). Surface tiers #F4F5F7, #EBEDF0. Divider #E4E6EB. Dark mode: canvas #15171A, chat backdrop #101418, dividers #262A30.
Bubbles: incoming white #FFFFFF (text #1A1A1A) with a clipped bottom-LEFT tail corner; outgoing a soft blue tint #DBEBFF (text a deep navy #14223A, not white) with a clipped bottom-RIGHT tail corner — both are asymmetric, mirror-image variants of each other, never symmetric.
Text: primary #1A1A1A / #ECEDEF, secondary #6B7280, tertiary #9AA0AA. All text/icons directly on the blue header bar are always white.
Semantic: notification/unread-badge/destructive red #F5325B (also used for timeline "like" hearts), success green #18A957 (also presence-online dot), warning amber #FF9500. A set of saturated mini-app tile colors (blue, green, orange, red, violet, cyan) exists but is contained strictly to the launcher grid.
Type ladder: Be Vietnam Pro, chosen specifically because it gives Vietnamese stacked tone marks proper vertical room (a generic Latin font clips them), with SF Pro as the iOS fallback. Line heights run deliberately generous (1.35-1.45) versus a typical Latin-only app. Screen title 24/700, list title 17/600, body/bubble 15/400, timestamp 11/600.
Corner radii: 5pt tail-clip corner, 8pt standard (buttons/cards/inputs), 12pt comfortable (sheets), 15pt mini-app launcher tiles, 16pt bubble body (3 of 4 corners), 19-20pt capsule inputs, full pill for action pills/badges/day-separators.
Distinctive named patterns: (1) a solid blue header bar that persists unchanged across every navigation push, functioning as a constant brand frame regardless of which screen is beneath it; (2) asymmetric clipped-tail bubbles (mirror-image incoming/outgoing) sitting on a distinct calm blue-grey chat backdrop; (3) a four-column grid of rounded-square saturated-color mini-app tiles as the super-app's service launcher; (4) Vietnamese-specific "Đã xem / Seen" read-receipt text and centered day-separator pills; (5) dense, super-app-scale list rows (72pt chat rows, 56pt settings rows) prioritizing scannable function over generous whitespace.
</reference_data>

<house_rules>
1. There is exactly one brand accent — the header blue — and it must never share top billing with a second saturated color anywhere in general chrome; mini-app tile colors are the one contained exception, scoped strictly to the launcher grid.
2. The solid blue header bar persists identically across every navigation push — never let it flash a different color or drop to a plain white/system bar mid-transition.
3. Bubbles are asymmetric mirror images of each other (clipped bottom-left for incoming, clipped bottom-right for outgoing) — never make them symmetric, and never swap which side is tinted.
4. Outgoing-bubble text is a deep navy ink on the soft blue tint, not white — the soft tint doesn't need reversed-contrast text the way a fully saturated bubble would.
5. Typography must give Vietnamese diacritics generous vertical room — never tighten a line-height to force a single-line row; let the row grow instead of clipping a tone mark.
6. The chat backdrop (a calm blue-grey) is a distinct token from the general white app canvas — don't conflate them; the backdrop exists specifically to separate white incoming bubbles from the surface behind them.
7. Saturated mini-app tile colors never leak outside the launcher grid into tab bars, headers, or general list rows.
8. Keep list rows dense on purpose (72pt chat, 56pt settings) — this is a super-app and scannable density is a deliberate choice, not a constraint to fight.
9. The only routine shadow in the system is a very soft lift under incoming white bubbles to separate them from the backdrop — everything else relies on hairline dividers and the solid header for structure.
</house_rules>
